newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Landsbergis eyes comeback as Lithuania votes.
newsitem.headline: Landsbergis eyes comeback as Lithuania votes.

text.p: The Baltic state of Lithuania voted in its second parliamentary election since quitting the former Soviet Union on Sunday with independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis hoping to unseat his bitter former Communist foes.

Lithuanians went to the polls under a leaden sky in a first round of elections for a parliament where remnants of huge graffiti-covered concrete barricades still stand as a reminder of the independence struggle.

Landsbergis, a stocky and bespectacled former music professor, was the unlikely hero of Lithuania's dramatic drive to leave the Soviet empire but was later rejected by voters as the country's economy struggled.

He is now leading his Homeland Union in a comeback bid by the right to unseat the ruling ex-Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP). Opinion polls suggest his group will be the largest in parliament.
Lithuanians choose from 24 parties and 1,531 candidates on Sunday and a second, run-off round is set for November 10.
Landsbergis, one of the first to vote, said he was choosing a "clean pair of hands", referring to his many accusations of corruption against the LDLP.
"I am voting for improvement and that means stability," he told reporters as he left the polling centre.

He and the Lithuanian people won many admirers when they stood up to Moscow, especially after 13 people were killed in a January 1991 assault by Soviet armed forces on the Vilnius television tower, a centre of resistance.

But as the economy plunged into crisis and inflation soared, his Sajudis movement was beaten at the ballot box in 1992 and the ex-Communists of the LDLP were propelled back to power. It was a bitter personal blow for Landsbergis.
The vote set a trend in eastern Europe, where people battered by economic transition voted for former Communists.
The LDLP's comeback was sealed in 1993 when leader Algirdas Brazauskas was elected president.
Brazauskas, now without party affiliation, seems set for a period of co-habitation with a right-wing government.
The broad-shouldered and ruddy-faced president said he hoped there would be no dramatic changes in Lithuania.
"The main thing is that we must have thoughtful people, who consider the future and not just their own political ambitions," he told journalists after voting.
Although the LDLP has made economic gains, opponents accuse it of corruption and croneyism.
People also became disillusioned by implementation of austerity policies set out by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The LDLP was badly hurt at the end of 1995 when a former prime minister withdrew his personal savings from a bank days before it was shut at the start of a banking crisis.
Lithuania has come a long way since Soviet days, with many of the trappings of a market economy visible in its capital, alive with new supermarkets, bars and Western cars.
But many people, especially pensioners, the unemployed and the low-paid have failed to benefit from the changes.
The Homeland Union has said it will work with the Christian Democrats but it is not certain which of the other parties likely to get it into parliament it can ally with.

Political commentators say Lithuanians, tired of the battle between Landsbergis and the LDLP and disillusioned by politics in general, may choose a "third force" or register a protest vote by backing more radical, fringe groups.
